name: Reducing alcohol and salt for eye redness

card.summary: Drinking less alcohol and eating less salt to get whiter, less bloodshot, less puffy eyes.
card.note: Persistent or painful red eye warrants medical assessment.

quick.overview:
This habit means cutting back on alcohol and salty food to see less red, bloodshot eyes and less puffiness.

People tend to notice the difference the morning after and adjust.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners say alcohol and salt are followed by redder eyes and puffiness. Red eye has many causes, including dry eye and irritation.
quick.risks: Low risk. Persistent redness, pain or vision changes call for a clinician.

lead: Reducing alcohol and salt for eye redness is a lifestyle habit in which people cut back on drinking and salty foods to get whiter, less bloodshot-looking eyes and a less puffy face. Clear sclera contribute to a rested, healthy look, and people in appearance communities track which habits show up in their eyes and face the next morning.

Red eye has many causes, including conjunctivitis, dry eye, irritants, tiredness, and medications or recreational drugs.[1] Practitioners report that nights with drinking or heavy salt are followed by redder eyes and facial puffiness. Wikipedia's general reference on red eye does not list alcohol or dietary sodium, so the specific link rests on personal reports; what the reference literature does describe is that alcohol has a dehydrating effect, is associated with vasodilation and disrupted sleep, and that excess dietary sodium can contribute to fluid retention.[2][3][4]
No published study has tested reduced alcohol or salt intake for eye redness itself.

chain: Drink less alcohol and eat less salt
Less dehydration, sleep disruption and fluid retention
Whiter, fresher-looking eyes and less facial puffiness
angle.text: People who notice redder eyes after drinking or salty meals cut back to see whiter, less puffy eyes. Sleep and hydration are commonly paired with the change.

paras: The habit means limiting alcohol, especially in the evening, and moderating salty or processed food, sometimes alongside more sleep and water. Users compare how their eyes and face look in the mornings after changes.

Wikipedia's hangover article states that ethanol has a dehydrating effect through increased urine production and lists vasodilation and sleep deprivation among factors in hangover; it does not mention bloodshot eyes.[2] The article on alcohol's effects on the body describes alcohol as limiting vasopressin release, disrupting sleep patterns and reducing sleep quality, particularly REM sleep, and says quitting is associated with restored hydration and improved skin appearance; it also describes the alcohol flush reaction, in which the face or body turns red from acetaldehyde build-up.[3]

Wikipedia's article on salt and health lists edema (fluid retention) as a possible effect of excess sodium and notes that reducing salt has been suggested as a way to treat it.[4] The WHO's 2020 guidance is no more than 5 g of salt (about 2 g of sodium) a day for adults, and the article also notes a U-shaped association between very low sodium intake and mortality.[4] The periorbital puffiness article likewise lists high dietary sodium among suggested causes of puffy eyes, though without a citation.[5]

Reference sources list conjunctivitis, dry eye, blepharitis, airborne irritants, tiredness and some drugs as causes, and note that eye pain, vision loss, light sensitivity or injury need urgent medical care.[1]
No studies found on reducing alcohol or salt intake for eye redness.
